justification: XSD 1.1 Part 2 §3.3.17.1-§3.3.17.2: the value space and the lexical space of xsd:anyURI are the finite-length sequences of zero or more characters, and the lexical mapping is the identity. So ""^^xsd:anyURI denotes the empty anyURI value.

XSD 1.1 Part 2 §4.3.1 and §4.3.2.3 (Validation Rule: minLength Valid, clause 1.1): anyURI length is measured in characters, and a value satisfies minLength n iff its length is at least n. The empty anyURI value has length 0, so it satisfies minLength 0 and violates minLength 1.
OWL 2 Structural Specification §4.6: the OWL 2 datatype map provides xsd:anyURI as specified by XML Schema, with xsd:minLength among its normative facets.

OWL 2 Direct Semantics §2.2.2 (Table 3): DatatypeRestriction(DT F lt) is (DT)^DT ∩ (F, lt)^FA, and DataComplementOf(DR) is Δ_D \ (DR)^DT. So anyURI[minLength 0] ∩ DataComplementOf(anyURI[minLength 1]) is exactly {""^^xsd:anyURI}.

OWL 2 Direct Semantics §2.2.3 (Table 4), §2.3.1, §2.3.6, §2.4 and §2.5: Δ_I = {a}, A = {a} and dp = {(a, ""^^xsd:anyURI)} satisfy ClassAssertion(A a) and the three SubClassOf axioms (both DataAllValuesFrom restrictions and DataMinCardinality(1 dp)). The ontology has a model, so it is consistent.
The pinned Java suite agrees elsewhere: AnyURITest.testSize_1 and testSize_3 assert that anyURI[length 0] is exactly {""}, a subset of this range.

Java cause: DatatypeChecker.DVariable.prepareAsValueSpaceSubset requires AnyURIValueSpaceSubset.hasCardinalityAtLeast(1), which counts the words of dk.brics.automaton 1.11-8 SpecialOperations.getFiniteStrings(automaton, 1). That method records a word only after following a transition, so it never reports the empty word of a non-singleton automaton. With the pinned jar, the difference built by conjoinWithDRNegation is non-empty, is not a singleton and accepts "", yet getFiniteStrings(1) returns no words. anyURI[length 0] is a singleton automaton, so testSize_1 and testSize_3 are counted correctly.

OWL 2 Structural Specification §9.5: HasKey(CE (OPE1 ... OPEm) (DPE1 ... DPEn)) has a separate object property list and data property list. The input HasKey(ObjectIntersectionOf(:A :B) (:r) (:dp)) has the data property :dp, and normalization must preserve the axiom's meaning, so the normalized key keeps (:dp). The pinned controls expect an empty data-property list. The sibling testKeys1 control keeps it: HasKey(:C (:r) (:dp)) normalizes to HasKey(<C> (<r> ) (<dp> )).

OWL 2 Direct Semantics §2.3.5 (Table 7): HasKey(CE (OPE...) (DPE...)) requires, for all named x and y that are instances of CE and share a value for every OPEi and every DPEj, that x = y. Dropping :dp makes the key identify individuals that agree only on :r, which the axiom does not entail.

The same condition applies the key to every named instance of CE, so a normalized key HasKey(K ...) with a fresh class K is equivalent only if CE ⊑ K. The pinned controls expect owl:Thing ⊑ :A ⊔ ¬K and owl:Thing ⊑ :B ⊔ ¬K, that is K ⊑ A ⊓ B, which is Java's normalization. Nothing forces an individual into K, so that key never applies: with :x and :y named instances of A ⊓ B sharing :r and :dp values and DifferentIndividuals(:x :y), the ontology is inconsistent under §2.3.5, but the faithful port of Java's normalization found it consistent. The corrected normal form is owl:Thing ⊑ K ⊔ ¬:A ⊔ ¬:B (A ⊓ B ⊑ K) with HasKey(K (:r) (:dp)); K ⊑ A ⊓ B is not needed, because the key clause tests K only in its body.
The trace's upstream_alternative control also has an unbalanced closing parenthesis in its second axiom, so it can match no normalization output; it is preserved unchanged as provenance.

Java cause: OWLNormalization.AxiomVisitor.visit(OWLHasKeyAxiom) passes axiom.getPropertyExpressions() through, so Java keeps :dp and fails both controls (the recorded Java failure at NormalizationTest.java:184). It replaces a complex key class CE by getDefinitionFor(positive(CE)) with the inclusion ¬K ⊔ CE, the direction used for a class in a positive position, although OWLClausification.clausifyKey places the key class in the clause body. The port instead defines K' ⊑ ¬CE and keys the simple complement ¬K' (which clausifyKey supports as a negated concept name); here K' is itself a negated definition, so the key class is <internal:def#0>.

reasoner.DateTimeTest.testFinite1_1.issue: none (known bug without an issue): xsd:dateTime 24:00:00 is 00:00:00 of the next day
justification: XSD 1.1 Part 2 §3.3.7.2 (dateTime lexical mapping) and §E.3.5 (dateTimeLexicalMap, through newDateTime): hour 24 is allowed only with zero minutes and seconds, and it maps to hour 0 of the next day. So 2000-12-31T24:00:00 and 2001-01-01T00:00:00 are two lexical forms of one value, with the same timezone offset if any.

XSD 1.1 Part 2 §E.3.1 and §3.3.7.2: the value has no hour 24 and no memory of the spelling, and the canonical mapping (§E.3.6) never produces 24:00:00, so the value is printed as 00:00:00 of the next day.

OWL 2 Structural Specification §4.7 (xsd:dateTime, xsd:dateTimeStamp) takes the value space and lexical mapping from XSD 1.1; OWL 2 Direct Semantics §2.2 interprets a literal as the value its lexical form maps to. So the two spellings denote one data value, and a range holding one of them holds exactly one value for it, not two.

The range xsd:dateTime[>= 1965-04-15T00:00:00, <= 1965-04-15T00:00:00] is one instant without a timezone offset, so it holds the single value 1965-04-15T00:00:00 (1965-04-14T24:00:00 is the same value). Two distinct values of it, as the test requires, cannot exist, so the ontology is inconsistent.

HermiT's DateTime keeps m_lastDayInstant for a lexical hour of 24 (DateTime.java:66) and compares it in equals, and DateTimeInterval.subtractSizeFrom and enumerateDateTimes count and list every local midnight a second time as 24:00:00 of the previous day. The pinned Java suite records those extra values.

reasoner.BinaryDataTest.testBase64Parsin.issue: none (known bug without an issue): an xsd:base64Binary literal denotes a base64Binary value

corrected.lexical: Z  X d y Z A ==

justification: OWL 2 Structural Specification §4.6 (Binary Data): the datatype map provides xsd:hexBinary and xsd:base64Binary, and states that their value spaces are disjoint. XSD 1.1 Part 2 §3.3.16 (base64Binary) gives base64Binary its own value space of finite octet sequences and a lexical mapping onto it.

OWL 2 Direct Semantics §2.2 interprets a literal as the value its datatype's lexical mapping assigns, so "ZXdyZA=="^^xsd:base64Binary denotes the base64Binary value with octets 65 77 72 64. It is a member of xsd:base64Binary, not of xsd:hexBinary, and differs from "65777264"^^xsd:hexBinary.

Java's assertion only checks the decoded octets (BinaryDataTest.assertBinaryData), which still hold: the corrected expectation is a base64Binary literal of the same octets, and the whitespace spelling decodes to the same value.

HermiT's BinaryData.parseBase64Binary returns new BinaryData(BinaryDataType.HEX_BINARY, data) (BinaryData.java:123), so the recorded trace prints a hexBinary value. As a result HermiT puts a base64Binary literal outside xsd:base64Binary (BinaryDataLengthInterval.contains compares the binary data type) and makes it equal to the hexBinary literal with the same octets.

reasoner.DatatypesTest.testINF.issue: none (known bug without an issue): Infinity is not an XSD lexical form of xsd:double

corrected.invalid: MalformedLiteralException: "Infinity" is not a well-formed value of datatype <http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema#double>

justification: XSD 1.1 Part 2 §3.3.5.1-§3.3.5.2: the lexical space of xsd:double is doubleRep, the decimal and scientific numerals plus the special values spelled INF, +INF, -INF and NaN (§3.3.5.2 lists these four spellings; doubleRep is noDecimalPtNumeral | decimalPtNumeral | scientificNotationNumeral | numericalSpecialRep, with numericalSpecialRep = '+INF' | '-INF' | 'INF' | 'NaN'). "Infinity" matches none of them, so "Infinity"^^xsd:double is not in the lexical space.

OWL 2 Structural Specification §4 and §5.7: OWL 2 takes xsd:double's lexical space and lexical-to-value mapping from XML Schema, and a literal whose lexical form is not in the lexical space of its datatype denotes no data value of the datatype map; it is ill-typed.

This project rejects an ontology holding an ill-typed literal of a supported datatype, as HermiT does with MalformedLiteralException for the literals its own parser refuses (DatatypesTest.testParsingError records that rejection for "4a"^^xsd:int). The test's ontology uses "Infinity"^^xsd:double in a DataOneOf and a NegativeDataPropertyAssertion, so it is rejected when the reasoner is created, and isConsistent has no answer: the replay expects the rejection (an invalid ontology, as recorded for testParsingError) instead of Java's false. The test meant the positive infinity; with the XSD spelling "INF"^^xsd:double the same axioms are inconsistent, as Java answered.

Java cause: DoubleDatatypeHandler.parseLiteral tries Double.parseDouble first, which accepts Java's own spellings Infinity, +Infinity and -Infinity (and surrounding whitespace), and falls back to INF and -INF only when it fails.
